description: Interested in space, technology, or data? Join our CLPS Lunar Mission Browser Challenge! We’re building an interactive browser to explore and visualize lunar mission data. We’re looking for teammates interested in coding, engineering, data analytics, UI/Design, research, and data management. No experience required—just bring your interest and willingness to learn.
summary:
Lunar Site Scout is a web tool that shows whether a lander at any spot on the Moon will have sunlight for power and a line of sight to Earth for communication. It was built by The Cosmic Cartel for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge.

Users pick a landing site and a landing date, then “fly” a 30-day mission. The site shows the Sun and Earth against the local horizon, countdowns to sunset and earthset, a simple battery model, a Moon map of current sunlight, a mission timeline, and a side-by-side comparison of sites and dates.

Positions are calculated with the open-source Astronomy Engine and the IAU 2015 lunar rotation model, and checked against NASA JPL Horizons, matching within 0.002° at Mons Mouton.

This matters because near the lunar south pole the Sun and Earth sit right on the horizon, so a small change in site or schedule can leave a lander without power or contact. Lunar Site Scout makes that risk visible in seconds, for mission planners and students alike.
details:
What it does and how it works
Lunar Site Scout is a website that shows whether a lander at any point on the Moon will have sunlight for power and a line of sight to Earth for radio contact. You pick a landing site (Apollo sites, recent landers, planned CLPS targets, or any point clicked on the Moon map), pick a landing date, and “fly” a 30-day mission. The site shows the Sun and Earth against the local horizon, countdowns to sunset and earthset, a simple battery and solar model, a Moon map of current sunlight, a 30-day timeline, a 12-month view of landing dates, and a table for comparing sites and dates side by side.

Behind the page, a server calculates the Sun’s and Earth’s position in the lunar sky every 15 minutes, using the open-source Astronomy Engine and the IAU 2015 lunar rotation model, which accounts for the Moon’s wobble (libration).

Benefits and intended impact
Near the lunar south pole the Sun and Earth sit right on the horizon, so a small change in site or schedule can leave a lander without power or contact. Our tool makes that visible in seconds instead of requiring specialist software. We want mission planners to be able to screen sites and dates quickly, and students to understand why polar landings are so difficult.

Tools and languages
JavaScript, HTML and CSS; Node.js with Express for the back end; HTML canvas for all the drawing; the Astronomy Engine library; NASA JPL Horizons for validation; NASA-derived Earth and Moon map imagery; Vercel for hosting. We used Claude (an AI assistant) for parts of the interface code, deployment and presentation materials, as described in our AI disclosure. [Add any other tools or hardware your team used.]

How it is creative
Rather than giving a table of angles, it lets you fly the mission and watch the outcome. Earth is drawn showing the side that actually faces the Moon at that moment, lit from the real Sun direction. A guided 5-step tour teaches the ideas using real missions such as Apollo 11 and Chandrayaan-3.

What we considered

  • Accuracy: we compared our results with JPL Horizons, matching within 0.002° at Mons Mouton across 24 sampled times.
  • Honesty about limits: no terrain is built in yet, so the horizon is a smooth sphere unless the user pastes a measured profile; “contact” means line of sight only; the battery model is for teaching, not a real power budget.
  • Ease of use: a Simple mode hides advanced settings, and the layout works on phones.
  • Next steps: built-in LOLA terrain, ground-station coverage, more languages, and a public API.
